title: Great Leaders Create Happiness to Make Themselves Happy
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece argues that the happiness of exceptional leaders is not incidental to their success but a direct byproduct of how invested they are in the satisfaction of the people they lead. The author contrasts this with leaders who treat their own team's happiness as irrelevant to results. The piece takes a clear position on a familiar chicken-and-egg question: exceptional leaders believe happy people become successful, rather than assuming success eventually produces happiness. The piece closes on a Charlie Chaplin quote to reinforce the idea that making others happy is a selfishly rewarding leadership habit.
points: Exceptional leaders' own happiness is framed as a direct byproduct of how invested they are in the satisfaction of the people they lead.
Leaders who dismiss team happiness as irrelevant to results aren't necessarily bad people, the piece frames it as a missed insight.
The piece takes a specific stance on a chicken-and-egg question, arguing happy people become successful rather than the reverse.
Caring about team happiness is explicitly distinguished from avoiding hard conversations.
quotes: But if you really want to understand why the best leaders are happy people, you need to comprehend how important it is for them to make others happy.
In their desire to create outstanding results and outcomes, they have to come to believe happiness gets in the way.
In the chicken and egg equation, they prefer to believe that happy people are more successful, and not that successful people are happier.
This is not to say great leaders feel responsible for others’ happiness or that they dodge challenging conversations or decisions because they might make others less satisfied or upset.
If the greatest happiness in the world is to make others happy, then great leaders are happy people.
